strengths: The manuscript presents a clear and potentially important idea: replacing pixel-history retrieval with a learned, dynamically evolving 3D state coupled to camera prediction and neural rendering. This decomposition is original and well motivated. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/eec2cdba93474c75ab3b8393fb60c9bf/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The system demonstrates useful capabilities that pixel-only generators do not naturally provide, including explicit 3D initialization, mid-rollout scene editing, and the evolution of off-screen processes.

The empirical results are promising: PERSIST substantially improves FVD and human ratings over the reported Oasis and WorldMem results, and the evaluation includes 148 rollouts across four behavior policies plus more than 800 human judgments from 28 participants.
The method is presented clearly, with helpful diagrams, inference pseudocode, architectural specifications, parameter counts, context sizes, training costs, and sampler settings.

The limitations discussion is unusually concrete and appropriately acknowledges dependence on simulator-provided 3D supervision, autoregressive drift, and loss of information outside the finite agent-centered volume. Figure 14 gives informative failure examples rather than concealing them.
weaknesses: The central causal claim—that persistent 3D state produces the reported improvements—is not adequately isolated. PERSIST is trained and evaluated in Luanti/Craftium, whereas Oasis and WorldMem use Minecraft data and are evaluated in MineDojo. Consequently, dataset, renderer, visual domain, training procedure, and possibly model capacity are confounded with representation type. FVD values computed against different target distributions are particularly unsuitable for direct method comparison.

The statement that Oasis can be viewed as an ablation with 3D guidance disabled is misleading unless an otherwise identical Oasis-style model was trained on the same Craftium trajectories with matched capacity and optimization. Such a controlled pixel-only ablation is missing, as are ablations of the camera model, projection mechanism, noise augmentation, and predicted versus ground-truth camera trajectories.

Evidence for geometric consistency and spatial memory is mostly subjective. The paper reports no simulator-grounded measures of camera error, voxel-state accuracy, revisit consistency, geometry preservation, collision correctness, or fidelity of off-screen dynamics, despite having ground-truth cameras and voxel states available. The off-screen dynamics and editability claims are supported mainly by selected examples.

The user study lacks essential statistical and procedural detail. It does not specify participant recruitment, compensation, consent or ethics review, pair allocation, presentation-side randomization, blinding, repeated-measures treatment, or what the reported ± values denote. The paper repeatedly says improvements are “significant” without reporting hypothesis tests, confidence intervals appropriate to participant-level dependence, or multiple-comparison handling.

The claimed long-horizon persistent memory is spatially bounded: only a 48^3 region centered on the agent is retained, and distant locations are explicitly forgotten. Thus the method provides fixed-cost local state rather than persistent memory of an arbitrarily explored world. Evaluations lasting 192 or 600 frames do not quantify behavior after leaving and later revisiting the retained region.

The demonstrated domain is a voxel simulator with direct semantic voxel and camera supervision. This is a useful test bed, but it makes projection and correspondence unusually accessible and leaves applicability to continuous geometry, deformable objects, real video, or photorealistic environments unverified. Several broader claims should therefore be narrowed.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite strong architectural documentation: there is no stated code, model, or dataset release; training steps, random seeds, exact data splits, policy probabilities, preprocessing details, inference speed, and hardware memory requirements are absent. The very large training budget also makes independent reproduction difficult.

Research-ethics treatment is too cursory. The impact statement reasonably notes the synthetic setting but does not discuss misuse of increasingly realistic interactive simulators or document ethical safeguards for the human-subject study.

strengths: Originality/significance: PERSIST presents a compelling decomposition of interactive generation into an evolving latent 3D world frame, camera prediction, geometric projection, and learned pixel rendering. Persistent editable state is useful for long-horizon simulation and offers capabilities that pixel-history models do not naturally provide.

Soundness: The system is demonstrated at substantial scale using approximately 40 million interactions, 148 evaluation trajectories, rollouts up to 2,000 steps, FVD, and a 28-participant user study. Reported improvements are large rather than marginal.
Presentation: The manuscript is generally clear and visually effective. Equations, inference algorithms, architecture tables, and qualitative illustrations make the pipeline understandable.
Reproducibility: The appendix provides useful model shapes, parameter counts, context lengths, sampler settings, optimization details, evaluation policies, and user-study instructions.

Limitations/ethics: The paper candidly identifies dependence on ground-truth 3D supervision, autoregressive drift, and finite spatial extent. Experiments use an open-source synthetic environment, limiting immediate privacy and data-collection concerns. weaknesses: Soundness: The decisive comparison is confounded. PERSIST is trained and evaluated on Luanti/Craftium, whereas Oasis and WorldMem are trained on Minecraft and evaluated through MineDojo. FVD is computed against each method's corresponding dataset, so differences may reflect environment appearance, data quality, policy distribution, or train-test mismatch rather than persistent 3D state. Human ratings across these visibly different domains are likewise not a controlled architectural comparison.

Soundness: The manuscript calls Oasis an ablation with 3D guidance disabled, but it is not a matched ablation: it was trained on different data and is not shown to match PERSIST in parameter count, optimization, compute, preprocessing, or auxiliary components. A same-data PERSIST variant with the world-frame pathway removed, plus matched pixel-memory and oracle-state controls, is necessary to support the central causal claim.

Soundness: The chosen quantitative metric does not establish long-horizon persistence. FVD is calculated on 16-frame clips even though the claimed advantage concerns revisitation and memory over hundreds or thousands of steps. There is no direct measurement of world-frame accuracy, 3D occupancy consistency, loop-closure/revisit fidelity, camera error, off-screen dynamics accuracy, or degradation as a function of rollout length.

Soundness: The user study does not justify the repeated claim of statistical significance. The paper omits pair counts per comparison, participant recruitment and screening, randomization/blinding details, the definition of the reported uncertainty, hypothesis tests, and analysis accounting for repeated ratings from only 28 participants. The head-to-head matrices report means without uncertainty or significance tests.

Originality: Closely related explicit-3D and persistent embodied world-model work is cited, notably Zhou et al. (2025), but the manuscript does not carefully articulate what is technically new relative to those systems. Much of the construction combines established flow-matching DiTs, voxel VAEs, camera tracking, rasterization, and deferred neural rendering.

Reproducibility/presentation: Important implementation information remains absent, including training iterations or stopping rules, dataset splits and release status, exact action-sequence distributions, voxel recentering/alignment as the agent moves, depth-peeling layer count, seeds, and code/checkpoint availability. Reproducing the reported system would also require unusually large compute.

Significance/generalization: Evaluation is restricted to one voxel-based game with privileged semantic 3D supervision. The fixed 48-cubed agent-centered state discards distant locations, so the claim of persistent spatial memory is local rather than open-ended. Editing and off-screen dynamics are supported primarily by selected qualitative examples.

Limitations/ethics: The limitations discussion is appropriately candid, but the impact statement is too cursory given the considerable training compute and possible downstream use of increasingly realistic interactive simulators. Environmental cost and broader misuse considerations are not discussed. Overall, the idea is promising, but the present evidence does not reliably attribute the gains to the proposed 3D persistence mechanism, preventing acceptance in its current form.

strengths: Originality: PERSIST presents a compelling decomposition of interactive world modeling into a learned persistent 3D world-frame, camera prediction, geometric projection, and pixel rendering. Replacing retrieved pixel histories with an actively updated spatial state is a meaningful conceptual contribution.

Significance: Persistent spatial memory is an important problem for interactive generation. The representation also enables useful capabilities that pixel-history models do not naturally provide, including explicit 3D initialization, mid-rollout scene editing, and modeling off-screen dynamics.

Soundness: The method is technically coherent, and experiments cover 148 held-out trajectories, four behavior modes, FVD, and more than 800 human evaluations from 28 participants. PERSIST substantially improves the reported human ratings and FVD, while the 2,000-step example transparently illustrates both long-horizon stability and failure modes.

Presentation: The manuscript is clear and polished. The architecture, inference algorithms, model sizes, context lengths, compute requirements, and evaluation protocol are described in useful detail, and the figures communicate the approach effectively.

Limitations and ethics: The paper appropriately acknowledges its dependence on ground-truth 3D supervision, finite spatial extent, and autoregressive drift. Its use of an open-source synthetic environment limits immediate societal risk.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central comparison is not controlled. PERSIST is trained and evaluated in Luanti/Craftium, whereas Oasis and WorldMem are evaluated using their Minecraft/MineDojo setting. FVD values computed against different reference distributions are not directly comparable, and engine-specific appearance and dynamics can also confound human ratings.

Soundness: The claim that improvements arise from the persistent 3D state lacks a matched ablation. Calling Oasis an ablation does not substitute for training PERSIST's own pixel model on the same data, architecture, optimization budget, and actions with only world-frame guidance removed. Comparisons to retrieval using the same camera estimates and training set would also be important.

Evaluation: The paper repeatedly describes differences as statistically significant, but reports no hypothesis tests, participant-level analysis, or clear definition of the displayed uncertainty. Ratings from multiple videos scored by the same 28 participants are correlated and should not be treated as independent observations.

Evaluation: Quantitative long-horizon evidence is limited. FVD uses 192-frame rollouts split into 16-frame clips, which primarily measures short-range quality and cannot establish persistent memory over the 600- or 2,000-step horizons emphasized by the paper. A direct revisit-memory or 3D-state accuracy metric is missing.

Significance/generalization: Training uses privileged semantic voxel grids from one voxel-based simulator. This is a reasonable research setting, but evidence does not yet establish applicability to general 3D scenes, non-voxel geometry, or real-world video; moreover, the 48-cubed agent-centered state discards distant locations rather than providing globally persistent memory.

Reproducibility and ethics: Architectural tables and compute accounting are helpful, but the manuscript does not state that code, trained models, dataset-generation scripts, or evaluation videos will be released, and some training details remain incomplete. The human-study description also omits recruitment, consent, compensation, and demographic information. These issues reduce independent reproducibility but appear remediable.

strengths: Originality and significance: PERSIST replaces pixel-history retrieval with an evolving latent 3D world frame, learned camera dynamics, geometric projection, and neural deferred rendering. This is a compelling formulation of persistent state for interactive video world models and enables useful capabilities such as 3D initialization and mid-rollout scene editing.

Soundness: The evaluation is substantial within Luanti: approximately 40M interactions, 100K trajectories, 168 held-out rollouts per method, horizons up to 600 frames, matched VAE/backbone/training conditions for quantitative baselines, and component ablations. PERSIST improves 600-frame FVD from 875 for Oasis and 247 for No-3D-Upscale to 148; the relatively flat FID trajectory also supports improved rollout stability.

The ablations are informative. The No-3D-Upscale result demonstrates the importance of high-resolution geometric projection, PERSIST-S probes spatial compression, Camera-GT examines learned camera dynamics, and PERSIST+w0 shows that additional aligned 3D information is effectively used.

The human study complements perceptual metrics with explicit ratings of visual fidelity, 3D consistency, and temporal consistency. Across more than 800 evaluations by 28 participants, PERSIST configurations consistently outperform the pixel-history baselines, although they remain clearly below ground truth.

Presentation is generally clear and polished. The decomposition, inference algorithms, architectural tables, qualitative long-rollout examples, and limitations discussion make the system understandable. The authors appropriately acknowledge ground-truth 3D supervision, exposure bias, finite spatial memory, and non-real-time inference.

No major application-level ethical concern is apparent because experiments use a synthetic, open-source game environment; the impact discussion is proportionate and does not overstate immediate deployment readiness.
weaknesses: The evidence does not fully isolate the central long-horizon spatial-memory claim. FVD is computed on 16-frame clips cut from the rollouts and FID is framewise, so neither directly measures whether a location is reconstructed consistently after a long absence. A controlled revisit metric, correspondence-based geometric error, or comparison of generated and ground-truth 3D states would be substantially more diagnostic.

Generality is limited to one voxel-based simulator with directly available semantic 3D supervision. Voxel grids make geometry, rasterization, and editing unusually convenient, and no experiment tests continuous geometry, real video, another simulator, or transfer across domains. Thus the broad framing as a paradigm for complex 3D environments is stronger than the demonstrated scope.

Several prominent capabilities are supported mainly by selected qualitative examples. Off-screen dynamics, collision reasoning, recovery over thousands of steps, diverse single-image 3D completion, and edit faithfulness lack systematic success rates or controlled quantitative evaluation. The paper itself shows local 3D drift, disappearing/appearing blocks, texture drift, and collision errors during the 2,000-step example.

The human-study comparison is confounded: released Oasis and WorldMem models are evaluated on Minecraft/MineDojo, whereas PERSIST is evaluated on Craftium/Luanti. Showing that ground-truth videos from the domains differ by less than 0.15 in average rating does not establish that model difficulty or artifact distributions are comparable. The study also omits inferential significance tests, interval definitions, participant compensation/consent or review procedures, and sufficient detail on randomization and blinding.

Some claims are overstated. Geometry is not consistent 'by construction' because the predicted latent world frame can drift and the learned pixel renderer can deviate from projected structure. Likewise, memory cost is independent of episode duration only because the method retains a finite agent-centered region and explicitly discards distant places; it does not yet provide global persistent memory.

Reproducibility is only moderate. Architectural and sampling hyperparameters and compute costs are reported, but the manuscript gives no clear code/model/data release commitment and insufficient detail about procedural-world generation, splits, training duration in updates, action-policy probabilities, metric implementation choices, and study materials. The very large stated training requirement also makes independent replication difficult.

At 2.67 seconds per frame for PERSIST-S with 20 denoising steps, the system is not interactive in the ordinary real-time sense. The faster setting reaches only 1.13 FPS and incurs a substantial FVD increase, reducing the immediate practical significance for embodied-agent simulation or interactive use.

strengths: Soundness: The persistent 3D-state formulation is coherent and technically substantial, combining learned world-frame dynamics, camera prediction, geometric projection, and pixel generation. On 168 held-out 600-frame trajectories, PERSIST substantially improves FVD over retrained pixel-history baselines, and the No-3D-Upscale and reduced-token ablations provide useful evidence that the 3D pathway matters.

Presentation: The method, inference pipeline, architectures, computational requirements, and principal design choices are explained clearly. Figures effectively communicate the model and its qualitative behavior.

Significance: Maintaining an editable, dynamically evolving 3D state enables useful capabilities unavailable to ordinary video-history models, including explicit 3D initialization, scene editing, and modeling events outside the current view. Stability over hundreds or thousands of frames is practically relevant.

Originality: Replacing retrieved pixel memories with an actively generated 3D latent state and learned deferred renderer is a meaningful architectural contribution, even though its components draw on established diffusion, voxel, and neural-rendering techniques.

The paper openly discusses important limitations, including dependence on supervised 3D data, finite spatial extent, exposure bias, and sub-real-time inference. The appendix provides extensive model and runtime details, and the user study complements automated metrics.
weaknesses: Soundness: The headline claims about spatial memory, geometric consistency, and off-screen causal dynamics are not evaluated with direct, task-specific measurements. FID/FVD mainly measure distributional appearance, while collisions, revisitation accuracy, camera drift, voxel-state accuracy, and off-screen evolution are supported principally by subjective ratings or selected examples.

The evaluation is confined to one Minecraft-like voxel engine where dense semantic 3D supervision and rasterization are unusually natural. This substantially limits evidence that the approach transfers to continuous geometry, real video, photorealistic environments, or settings without privileged simulator state.

The human-study baseline comparison is confounded: the released Oasis and WorldMem models are evaluated on MineDojo, whereas PERSIST is evaluated on Craftium/Luanti. Similar ratings for ground-truth videos do not establish that model difficulty and artifacts are comparable across domains. The study also omits statistical testing, the meaning of the reported error bars, treatment of repeated ratings from the same 28 participants, and recruitment/consent details.

Baseline coverage is incomplete for isolating the central mechanism. There is no static-3D-state baseline, oracle world-state rollout, explicit world-model accuracy evaluation, or convincing comparison to the cited prior work on persistent 3D embodied world models. WorldMem results beyond 200 generated frames are absent without sufficient explanation.

Reproducibility is limited by the enormous training budget and missing operational details such as training steps or stopping criteria, random seeds and run-to-run variability, precise environment generation and split definitions, evaluation code, and a concrete code/data release statement.

Significance is curtailed by the fixed 48-cubed agent-centered state: distant locations are discarded, so the system does not provide persistent memory over arbitrarily large environments despite some broad wording about long-horizon spatial memory. Even the accelerated configuration runs at only about 1.13 FPS.

The impact statement is overly cursory. A synthetic training domain reduces immediate risks but does not remove concerns associated with deployment in embodied-agent training, digital twins, simulation bias, or generated interactive content.

strengths: Soundness: The core decomposition into a dynamic latent voxel world, learned camera model, geometric projection, and neural pixel renderer is technically coherent. Conditioning the renderer on pixel-aligned, depth-ordered 3D features is a particularly well-motivated design.

Evidence: Results on 168 held-out trajectories are strong and consistent. PERSIST improves 600-frame FVD from 875 for Oasis to 148, while its FID remains comparatively stable; ratings from 28 participants and over 800 evaluations also favor PERSIST on visual fidelity, 3D consistency, temporal consistency, and overall quality.

Ablations provide useful causal evidence. No-3D-Upscale performs substantially worse, PERSIST-S tests spatial compression, Camera-GT examines learned camera dynamics, and PERSIST+w0 demonstrates that informative aligned 3D initialization yields further gains.

Significance and originality: Maintaining and evolving an explicit learned 3D state, rather than retrieving observations from a pixel history, is a meaningful contribution to interactive world modeling. It enables useful capabilities such as direct 3D initialization, mid-rollout scene editing, and simulation of off-screen processes.

Presentation is clear and visually effective. The manuscript explains the pipeline, training objectives, architectures, inference algorithms, compute requirements, and study protocol in substantial detail. It also candidly discusses dependence on 3D supervision, exposure bias, bounded spatial memory, artifacts, and sub-real-time inference.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is limited to one voxel-based game engine with privileged semantic voxel supervision. Consequently, the results establish the approach within Luanti but do not yet demonstrate that it transfers to photorealistic, non-voxel, partially observed, or real-world environments.

The main automated metrics do not directly measure the central geometric and spatial-memory claims. FVD is computed from independent 16-frame clips and timestep-wise FID is largely insensitive to whether revisited locations retain their geometry. Direct voxel accuracy, camera error, loop-closure consistency, collision accuracy, and controlled revisit tests would provide stronger evidence.

Several novel capabilities, especially persistent off-screen dynamics, causal emergence, and precise 3D editing, are supported mainly by selected qualitative examples. Broader quantitative tests are needed to establish their reliability rather than possibility.

Comparisons do not fully control for model capacity and privileged supervision: PERSIST adds large world and camera components beyond the pixel-only baselines. Moreover, the human study uses released Oasis and WorldMem models in Minecraft/MineDojo while PERSIST is evaluated in Craftium, and WorldMem receives 600 ground-truth observations for initialization. The ground-truth domain check helps but does not eliminate these model-, training-, and domain-level confounds.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful architecture tables. The paper does not provide a code/data release statement, training-step counts or stopping criteria, random-seed variation, full loss and augmentation details, or sufficiently precise procedural-world splits. The very large compute requirement also makes independent replication difficult.

The human-study analysis lacks significance tests or a model accounting for repeated ratings by the same participants, and it does not clearly define the reported uncertainty intervals. Recruitment, compensation, consent, and ethics-review details are also absent.

Claims such as fixed-cost persistent spatial memory and geometric consistency 'by construction' should be qualified: the maintained world covers only a finite 48-cubed region centered on the agent, distant locations are forgotten, and the generated 3D state itself demonstrably drifts. Inference also remains slow at roughly 2.67 seconds per frame in the reported main-speed configuration.
